newsitem.title: CHINA: China rubber futures confrontation ends,mkt falls.
newsitem.headline: China rubber futures confrontation ends,mkt falls.

text.p: The confrontation between traders who are long and short on the China rubber futures market has been broken with another round of price falls in sight, traders said on Monday.
After two weeks of consolidation, the key August 1997 contract fell on enlarged volume ahead of Friday's close after players with new short positions pushed down prices, they said.
The contract opened last week's trading at 11,225 yuan ($1,354) per tonne and moved in a narrow range for the first two days.
But it plunged on Friday to end the week at 10,790 yuan per tonne, down 435 yuan.
The rubber market closed last Monday and Tuesday to mark the reversion of Hong Kong from British to Chinese rule.
Open interest in the August contract surged to a record high of more than 190,000 lots from 174,434 lots the previous week.
One lot is five tonnes of rubber on the China Commodity Futures Exchange in Haikou, capital of the southern island province of Hainan.
"Both technical charts and fundamentals are in favour of shorts after the plunges on Friday," said one trader with a major futures brokerage in Hainan.
"But major shorts were not seen taking part in pushing down prices and there are also no signs that the big longs will retreat," he said.
"Selling by medium and small investors moved the market," the trader added.
The exchange's rubber stock had grown to around 75,000 tonnes from 72,989 tonnes a week ago, traders said.

They said although the confrontation between longs and shorts had been broken and the trend for the time being was for further falls, longs still had the capacity to compete with shorts and pull up prices once again.

"Long position holders believe the spot price, which has fallen to 10,000 yuan per tonne, will consolidate around that level in the short term, and they may push up prices to force speculative sellers to offset their positions despite losses," one Shanghai trader said.
"The recent falls might be a trap set by the longs to lure retail short-sellers, and they are still likely to push up prices to squeeze profits from these retail sellers," another Hainan trader said.
